stem:
Sipho finds the relative atomic mass of a Group 2 metal M from the volume of hydrogen it gives with excess dilute hydrochloric acid at room conditions:

$\ce{M(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> MCl2(aq) + H2(g)}$

He weighs a strip of M (by difference, balance reading to 0.001 g), drops it into 25 cm³ of 1 mol dm⁻³ HCl in a conical flask, quickly replaces the bung connected to a 250 cm³ gas syringe and records the final volume of gas (syringe read to ±0.5 cm³). He repeats with strips of different mass.

| Mass of M / g | 0.040 | 0.060 | 0.080 | 0.100 | 0.120 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Volume of hydrogen / cm³ | 40 | 59 | 72 | 99 | 118 |

Molar volume of a gas at room conditions = 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Sipho's table follows the usual conventions. State two conventions for recording raw data in a results table.

points.description: Each column (or row) heading has the quantity and its unit separated by a solidus (e.g. mass of M / g)
All readings of one quantity to the same number of decimal places, matching the precision of the instrument (0.001 g; whole cm³ or to 0.5 cm³)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Headings give the quantity and unit (mass of M / g, volume / cm³), and each set of readings is recorded to the same, appropriate precision: masses to 0.001 g, volumes to the precision of the syringe.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe the graph Sipho should draw to analyse his results (axes, scale and line).

points.description: Volume of hydrogen (y-axis) against mass of M (x-axis), with labelled axes and units, scales using more than half the grid
A straight best-fit line through the origin, ignoring the anomalous point

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Plot volume of hydrogen / cm³ on the y-axis against mass of M / g on the x-axis, choosing scales that use most of the grid, then draw a straight line of best fit through the origin that ignores the anomalous point.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Give the mass, in g, of the strip whose result is anomalous.
parts.explanation: The 0.080 g point (72 cm³) lies well below the line; about 79 cm³ was expected.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest a reason for the anomalous result and how the method could be changed to avoid it.

points.description: Some hydrogen escaped before the bung was replaced (or the apparatus leaked / the strip was partly oxidised)
Place the metal in a small tube inside the flask (or tie it to the bung) and tip it into the acid after the bung is in place / check joints for leaks

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Some hydrogen probably escaped before the bung was replaced. The strip could be held in a small tube or suspended from the bung so that it falls into the acid only after the apparatus is sealed.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Determine the gradient of the best-fit line through the origin, in cm³ g⁻¹ (exclude the anomaly).
parts.explanation: Best-fit line through the origin: gradient ≈ 986 cm³ g⁻¹ (for example 118 ÷ 0.120 ≈ 983). Any value within ±30 of this is accepted.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Best-fit line through the origin: gradient ≈ 986 cm³ g⁻¹ (for example 118 ÷ 0.120 ≈ 983). Any value within ±30 of this is accepted.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Use your gradient to calculate the relative atomic mass of M.
parts.explanation: 1 mol M gives 1 mol H₂ = 24 000 cm³, so V = (m ÷ Ar) × 24 000 and the gradient = 24 000 ÷ Ar. Ar = 24 000 ÷ 986 = 24.3.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 1 mol M gives 1 mol H₂ = 24 000 cm³, so V = (m ÷ Ar) × 24 000 and the gradient = 24 000 ÷ Ar. Ar = 24 000 ÷ 986 = 24.3.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: The mass of each strip is found by difference from two balance readings, each ±0.001 g. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of the 0.040 g strip.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: The syringe is read at the start and end, each ±0.5 cm³. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the 40 cm³ volume.

parts.label: (j)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage difference between your value of Ar and the accepted value, 24.3.
parts.explanation: |24.3 − 24.3| ÷ 24.3 × 100 ≈ 0.1% (depends on your gradient; within the uncertainties of the method).
parts.workedSolution: 1. |24.3 − 24.3| ÷ 24.3 × 100 ≈ 0.1% (depends on your gradient; within the uncertainties of the method).

parts.label: (k)
parts.stem: Identify one systematic error and one random error in this experiment, explaining the effect of the systematic error on Ar.

points.description: Systematic: an oxide coating on the metal (or some hydrogen dissolving in / the acid adding volume, or gas temperature above room temperature)
Effect: e.g. oxide gives less hydrogen per gram, so the gradient is smaller and Ar too high (consistent direction explained)
Random: judging the syringe reading / timing of replacing the bung / small variations in strip mass

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A systematic error is a layer of magnesium oxide on the strips: the oxide reacts without giving hydrogen, so every strip gives less gas than expected, the gradient is too small and the calculated Ar is too high. A random error is the variable amount of gas lost while the bung is replaced, which scatters the points about the line.

parts.label: (l)
parts.stem: Suggest three improvements to the method.

points.description: Clean the metal with emery paper to remove the oxide layer
Use a method that seals the apparatus before the reaction starts (metal in a suspended tube / tipped in)
Use larger masses (within the syringe capacity) or a more precise balance to reduce percentage uncertainty; repeat each mass and average

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Rub each strip with emery paper to remove oxide; start the reaction only after the apparatus is sealed, for example by tipping the metal in from a small tube; and use the largest masses the 250 cm³ syringe allows, repeating each mass to average the results.

points.description: No naked flames near the apparatus because hydrogen is flammable

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Wear eye protection when handling the acid, and keep naked flames away because hydrogen is flammable.

explanation: Gradient ≈ 986 cm³ g⁻¹; Ar ≈ 24.3 (magnesium); anomaly at 0.080 g.
hints: A difference of two readings doubles the absolute uncertainty.
